To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the Rocky Mountains of British Columbia are a complex region with multiple thrust systems that have been active for at least 100 Ma and are still being reactivated.

(a) the structural interpretation of a 10,000 km2 area of the northern Canadian Rockies is presented; (b) the area is subdivided into three structural subprovinces, each with a distinct style of deformation, and (c) the structural evolution of the area is discussed in terms of the development of a foreland fold-and-thrust belt

(1) a large number of flat thrust faults occur beneath the western margin and within the Foothills and (2) a decollement in the Besa River shale separates these faults from those beneath the eastern margin of, and extending across, the Rocky Mountain subprovinces.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the following: (1) the structural and stratigraphic relationships between the Foothills and Rocky Mountains; (2) the nature of thrusting and associated structures; (3) the nature of the decollement; (4) the nature of deformation within the decollement and the nature of the deformation front; and (5) the nature of structures in the Foothills.

the following: (1) the structural style of the northern Canadian Rocky Mountains and (2) the nature of the transition between the Foothills and Rocky Mountains subprovinces of the northern Canadian Rockies, British Columbia.
the structural interpretation of a part of the Canadian Rocky Mountains.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the northern Canadian Rocky Mountains consist of a structurally complex Fohills subprovince of box and chevron style folds, and an apparently structurally simple Rocky Mountain subprovince of open folds and inconspicuous faults, separated by a narrow transition interval.

the northern Canadian Rocky Mountains are a region of structural complexity, with the following major features: (1) a major eastward-dipping thrust fault system beneath the Rocky Mountain subprovinces, (2) a major east-dipping thrust fault beneath the eastern margin of this subprovince, (3) a major east- and southeast-dipping thrust fault in the Foothills, (4) a major east-northeast-dipping thrust fault at the eastern margin of these mountains, (5)

the northern Rocky Mountains of British Columbia are characterized by: 1. a Foothills sub province with large amplitude box and/or chevron style folds, 2. a Rocky Mountain sub province with open folds and inconspicuous faults, and 3. a transition interval of more penetratively folded shales and thin bedded carbonates of late Devonian to Mississippian ages.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have shown that the northern Canadian Rocky Mountain subprovince is a structurally diverse region with a complex structural history.
the structural style in the northern Rocky Mountains is dominated by a combination of thrust faults with a relatively small amount of strike-slip displacement.
we have been able to define the structural style of this region and to show how the structural features relate to the geology.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the Rocky Mountain Front is a major crustal-scale structure.
the Rocky Mountains are not a single, continuous mountain chain, but rather are a series of mountain chains separated by intervening basins.
the mountain front in the northern Canadian Rockies is a thrust, not an erosional feature.
